claims.text: Dual-phase lamellar colonies in eutectic high-entropy alloys contain internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Microcrack initiation at internal boundaries contributes to room-temperature brittleness.
A minor dopant addition can preferentially segregate to lamellar-colony boundaries.
Preferential boundary segregation of the dopant will simultaneously increase strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
A refractory-metal or rare-earth dopant should be introduced during alloy processing.
Suitable processing and heat treatment can promote dopant segregation to colony boundaries.
The dopant concentration must remain low enough to avoid detrimental intermetallic formation.
Dopant-enriched boundary regions will alter local boundary chemistry.
The altered boundary chemistry will improve interfacial cohesion.
Dopant segregation enhances interfacial bonding and reduces microcrack nucleation.
Boundary modification strengthens the interface.
Boundary modification increases ductility by blunting crack-propagation paths.
The doped alloy will have greater yield strength than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The doped alloy will have greater ultimate tensile strength than the unmodified baseline.
The doped alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the unmodified baseline.
The predicted mechanical improvements arise from reduced microcracking and stabilization of two-phase interfaces.
The intervention is effective only within a dopant-concentration window that promotes segregation without producing brittle intermetallic compounds.
The intervention requires thermal processing that enables the intended segregation behavior.
A failure to obtain statistically significant improvements exceeding approximately 10% in both tensile strength and elongation to failure would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to verify dopant segregation at colony boundaries would falsify the hypothesis.
